1000436.etyen:
Ultimately from Middle Low German Frankrīke (“realm of the Franks; France”), from Old Saxon *Frankrīki. The Old Saxon form is composed of Proto-West Germanic *Frankō (“a Frank”) and *rīkī (“realm, kingdom”), literally “realm of the Franks”.
Synchronically equivalent to the stem of franker (“Frank”) + rike (“realm, kingdom”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Frankrike, Danish Frankrig, Swedish Frankrike, Low German Frankriek, Dutch Frankrijk and German Frankreich (“France”).

1005044.etyen:
A fixed phrase consisting of the imperative ha (“to have”), the pronoun det (“it”) and adverbial fint (“well, nicely”), the neuter singular of fin (“fine, nice”), literally “have it nice”. As a farewell, the phrase expresses a wish for the addressee's continued well-being.
The final part fin (“fine, nice”) is from late Old Norse fínn (“fine, polished”), ultimately from Latin finis (“end, limit”), with the semantic development through the sense “finished, perfected”.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk ha det fint and Danish have det fint (“to be well, be doing well”).
